title: 1 Chronicles 27:25–34
context: The stewards over David’s treasuries, fields, vineyards, olive groves, herds, and flocks, followed by the king’s counselors and officials, including Ahithophel, Hushai, Abiathar, and Joab, figures known from 2 Samuel.

verses.text: Over the king’s treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel. Over the treasures in the fields, in the cities, in the villages, and in the towers was Jonathan the son of Uzziah;
verses.arminianNotes: Azmaveth son of Adiel is over the king’s treasures, and Jonathan son of Uzziah over treasures in fields, cities, villages, and towers. Arminian readers see careful stewardship of the kingdom’s resources.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see orderly administration of royal property. The list of stewards shows the practical side of David’s rule alongside worship and defense.

verses.text: Over those who did the work of the field for tillage of the ground was Ezri the son of Chelub.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezri son of Chelub oversees those who till the ground. Arminian readers see agricultural work recognized as part of the kingdom’s well-being, worthy of faithful oversight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see ordinary labor organized within David’s administration. Readers in this tradition value the reminder that daily work is part of a well-ordered life under God.

verses.text: Over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite. Over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite.
verses.arminianNotes: Shimei the Ramathite oversees the vineyards, and Zabdi the Shiphmite the wine cellars. Arminian readers see responsibility divided carefully among capable stewards.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the detailed organization of the king’s holdings. The hometown names identify these officials, though some locations are uncertain.

verses.text: Over the olive trees and the sycamore trees that were in the lowland was Baal Hanan the Gederite. Over the cellars of oil was Joash.
verses.arminianNotes: Baal Hanan the Gederite oversees the olive and sycamore trees in the lowland, and Joash the oil cellars. Arminian readers see the land’s produce cared for responsibly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see stewardship of God’s good gifts in creation. Readers in this tradition note the practical wisdom behind assigning separate overseers to each resource.

verses.text: Over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite. Over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai.
verses.arminianNotes: Shitrai the Sharonite oversees herds in Sharon, and Shaphat son of Adlai herds in the valleys. Arminian readers see attention to livestock as an important part of the kingdom’s economy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the careful division of responsibilities by region. The record shows David’s administration reaching into every area of the nation’s life.

verses.text: Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite. Over the donkeys was Jehdeiah the Meronothite. Over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagrite.
verses.arminianNotes: Obil the Ishmaelite oversees the camels, Jehdeiah the donkeys, and Jaziz the Hagrite the flocks. Arminian readers note that non-Israelites served in David’s administration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see foreigners entrusted with royal responsibilities. Readers in this tradition note that the text records this without comment, suggesting that skill and trustworthiness were valued.

verses.text: All these were the rulers of the property which was King David’s.
verses.arminianNotes: “All these were the rulers of the property which was King David’s.” Arminian readers see the stewards’ list summarized, highlighting the scale of royal resources.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the summary closing the list of royal stewards. The orderly management of property reflects the stability God had given to David’s kingdom.

verses.text: Also Jonathan, David’s uncle, was a counselor, a man of understanding, and a scribe. Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king’s sons.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan, David’s uncle, is a counselor and scribe, and Jehiel son of Hachmoni is with the king’s sons. Arminian readers see wisdom and learning valued in the royal court.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see trusted family members and teachers serving the king. Readers in this tradition note that the Hebrew term for “uncle” can sometimes mean a broader relative, so the exact relation is uncertain.

verses.text: Ahithophel was the king’s counselor. Hushai the Archite was the king’s friend.
verses.arminianNotes: “Ahithophel was the king’s counselor. Hushai the Archite was the king’s friend.” Arminian readers recall their roles in Absalom’s revolt in 2 Samuel 15–17, where loyalty was tested.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the names recalling those events. The Chronicler lists them without retelling the revolt, and readers in this tradition do not harmonize the two accounts here.

verses.text: After Ahithophel was Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar. Joab was the captain of the king’s army.
verses.arminianNotes: After Ahithophel came Jehoiada son of Benaiah and Abiathar, and “Joab was the captain of the king’s army.” Arminian readers see the court list closing with key advisers and the army commander.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the leadership of David’s kingdom summarized. “Jehoiada the son of Benaiah” reverses the more familiar pairing of these names, and the text does not explain the relationship.
